standardized_question: Example 1.4. How long will it take \$3,000 to earn \$60 interest at 6%?
standardized_answer:
Solution. We have $P = 3000$, $I = 60$, $r = 0.06$, and then

$$
t = \frac{I}{Pr} = \frac{60}{3000 \cdot 0.06} = \frac{1}{3} \text{ years} = 4 \text{ months}.
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.14. A debt of $\$5,000$ is due at the end of 5 years. It is proposed that $\$X$ be paid now and with another $\$X$ paid in 10 years’ time to liquidate the debt. Calculate the value of $X$ if the effective interest rate is $12\%$ for the first 6 years and $8\%$ for the next 4 years.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The value of the first payment at time $t = 5$ is $X \cdot (1.12)^5$. The value of the second payment at time $t = 5$ is $X \cdot (1.08)^{-4} \cdot (1.12)^{-1}$. We equate the sum of these two values and the value of the debt of $\$5,000$ at $t = 5$ to obtain

$$
5000 = X \cdot (1.12)^5 + X \cdot (1.08)^{-4} \cdot (1.12)^{-1} = X \cdot (1.76234 + 0.656277) = 2.41862X
$$

Hence, $X = \$5,000 / 2.41862 \cong \$2,067.30$.

standardized_question: Example 1.10. Determine rates $i^{(2)}$ and $i^{(12)}$ that are equivalent to $r = 6\%$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. We equate the annual accumulation factors at each interest rate to obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}
(1 + i^{(2)} / 2)^2 &= e^{0.06} \qquad & (1 + i^{(12)} / 12)^{12} &= e^{0.06} \\
i^{(2)} / 2 &= e^{0.06 / 2} - 1 \qquad & i^{(12)} / 12 &= e^{0.06 / 12} - 1 \\
i^{(2)} &\cong 6.091\% \qquad & i^{(12)} &\cong 6.015\%
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.15. Suppose you can buy a house for $84,000 cash (option 1) or for payments of $50,000 now, $20,000 in 1 year, and $20,000 in 2 years (option 2). If money is worth $i^{(12)} = 9\%$, which option is more profitable?
standardized_answer:
Solution. The discounted value of option 1 is $84,000. Using monthly compounding, the discounted value of option 2 is

$$
\begin{aligned}
& 50,000 + 20,000 \cdot (1 + 0.09/12)^{-12} + 20,000 \cdot (1 + 0.09/12)^{-24} \\
& \cong 50,000 + 8,284.76 + 16,716.63 = 85,001.39.
\end{aligned}
$$

Clearly, option 1 is more preferable than option 2.

standardized_question: Example 1.16. If you file your taxes late, the Canada Revenue Agency charges you an immediate 5% late penalty, as well as $5\%$ compounded daily on your outstanding balance. Express my total penalty as a single rate (compounded daily) assuming I pay 26 weeks late.
standardized_answer:
Solution. If I pay $n$ days late, every dollar I originally owed swells to

$$
1.05 \cdot (1 + 0.05/365)^n.
$$

Therefore, on a per dollar basis my total debt after $n = 26 \cdot 7 = 182$ days is

$$
1.05 \cdot (1 + 0.05/365)^{182}.
$$

Had I been charged the single rate $i^{(365)}$, my total debt would have been $(1 + i^{(365)}/365)^{182}$. Equating and solving for $i^{(365)}$ we get

$$
1.05 \cdot (1 + 0.05/365)^{182} = (1 + i^{(365)}/365)^{182},
$$

which can be rearranged to find

$$
i^{(365)} = 365 \cdot \left( 1.05^{1/182} \cdot \left(1 + 0.05/365\right) - 1 \right) \cong 0.14787.
$$

Therefore my effective penalty rate is approximately $14.79\%$.

standardized_question: Example 1.19. You make deposits of $1,500 every six months starting today into a fund that pays interest at $i^{(2)} = 7\%$. How much do you have in your fund immediately after the 30th deposit?
standardized_answer:
Solution. We have $C = 1500$, $n = 30$, and the interest rate $0.07/2 = 0.035$ per half year. Since we have been asked to determine the accumulated value on the date of the 30th deposit, we deal with an ordinary simple annuity. Therefore,

$$
V_A = 1500 \cdot \frac{(1.035)^{30} - 1}{0.035} \cong \$77,434.02.
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.17. You have access to an account that pays $100r\%$ per annum, compounded annually. You are given two options to repay a debt. Option $A$ is an immediate payment of $\$30,000$; option $B$ is the payment of $\$16,000$ per year for each of the next two years. For what values of $r$ would you choose option $B$?
standardized_answer:
Solution. The present value of $B$, in thousands of dollars, is

$$
P_B(r) = \frac{16}{1 + r} + \frac{16}{(1 + r)^2}.
$$

The present value of $A$, in thousands of dollars, is $P_A(r) = 30$. It is only sensible to choose option $B$ provided $P_B(r) < P_A(r)$, which occurs if and only if

$$
30 > \frac{16}{1 + r} + \frac{16}{(1 + r)^2} \Longleftrightarrow 30(1 + r)^2 > 16(1 + r) + 16,
$$

which clearly occurs if and only if $30r^2 + 44r - 2 > 0$. The roots of this quadratic are $r \cong -1.510$ and $r \cong 0.0441$, and since the leading coefficient of the quadratic is positive we should therefore choose option $B$ if $r$ exceeds the larger root. In summary, we choose $A$ if the interest rate is less than (approximately) $4.41\%$ and choose $B$ otherwise. □

standardized_question: Example 1.12. Calculate the accumulated value of \$1,000 at the end of 4 years if $r(t) = 0.05 + 0.01t$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The accumulation function is

$$
A(T) = \exp \left( \int_0^T r(t) \, dt \right) = \exp \left( \int_0^T (0.05 + 0.01t) \, dt \right) = e^{0.05T + 0.05T^2}
$$

for every $T \geqslant 0$. Thus, after 4 years we have

$$
A(4) = e^{0.05 \cdot 4 + 0.05 \cdot 4^2} = e \cong 2.71828182
$$

and $V(4) = P A(4) = 1000 e \cong \$2,718.28$.

standardized_question: Example 1.22. Determine the discounted value and the accumulated value of $\$400$ payable semi-annually at the beginning of each half-year over 10 years if interest is 8% per year payable semi-annually.
standardized_answer:
Solution. We deal with an annuity due. There are $n = 20$ payment periods. The interest rate over one period of 6 months is $0.08 / 2 = 0.04$. Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_A &= 400 \frac{1.04^{20} - 1}{0.04} (1 + 0.04) = 400 \cdot 30.9692 \cong \$12,387.68, \\
P_A &= 400 \frac{1 - 1.04^{-20}}{0.04} (1 + 0.04) = 400 \cdot 14.1339 \cong \$5,653.58.
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.20. It is estimated that a machine will need replacing 10 years from now at a cost of $80,000. How much must be put aside each year to provide that amount of money if the company’s savings earn interest at an 8% annual effective rate?
standardized_answer:
Solution. Assume that an amount of $C$ is deposited at the end of each of 10 years. So we deal with an ordinary simple annuity. The accumulated value is

$$
V_A = C \frac{(1.08)^{10} - 1}{0.08} = \$80,000.
$$

Hence, $C \cong \$5,522.36$.

standardized_question: Example 1.25 (Interest is compounded more frequently than payments are made). Joe deposits $200 at the beginning of each year into a bank account that earns interest at $i^{(4)} = 6\%$. How much money will be in his bank account at the end of 5 years?
standardized_answer:
Solution. First, determine the rate $j$ per year equivalent to the rate of 0.06/4 per quarter:

$$
1 + j = (1 + 0.06/4)^4 \implies j = 1.015^4 - 1 \implies j = 6.136355\%
$$

Second, calculate the accumulated value $V_A$ of an ordinary annuity due with $C = \$200$, $n = 5$, and $j = 6.136355\%$:

$$
V_A = 200 \left( \frac{(1 + j)^6 - 1}{j} - 1 \right) = 200 \cdot 5.99931 \cong \$1,199.86.
$$

standardized_question:
Example 1.26 (Payments are made more frequently than interest is compounded).

A car is purchased by paying $2,000$ down and then $300$ each quarter for 3 years. If the interest on the loan was $i^{(2)} = 9.2\%$, what did the car sell for?
standardized_answer:
Solution. First, determine the rate $j$ per quarter equivalent to $0.092/2$ per half-year:

$$
(1 + j)^4 = (1 + 0.092/2)^2 \implies 1 + j = \sqrt{1.046} \implies j = 2.27414\%
$$

Second, calculate the discounted value $P$ of an ordinary simple annuity with $C = 300$, $n = 3 \cdot 4 = 12$, and $j = 2.27414\%$:

$$
P_A = 300 \frac{1 - (1 + j)^{-12}}{j} = 300 \cdot 10.39946 \cong 3,119.84.
$$

The sale price of the car is $P = 2,000 + P_A = 5,119.84$.

standardized_question: Example 1.30. A corporation issues 15-year bonds redeemable at par. Under the contract, interest payments will be made at the rate $c^{(2)} = 10\%$. The bonds are priced to yield 8% per annum compounded monthly. What is the issue price of a \$1,000 bond?
standardized_answer:
Solution. We have $F = W = \$1,000$, $c = 0.1 / 2 = 0.05$, $n = 15 \cdot 2 = 30$. Calculate rate $j$ per half-year equivalent to $i^{(12)} = 8\%$:

$$
(1 + j)^2 = \left(1 + \frac{0.08}{12}\right)^{12} \implies j = \left(1 + \frac{0.08}{12}\right)^6 - 1 \implies j = 0.040672622.
$$

Now the purchase price is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= W + (Fc - Wj)a_{\overline{30}|j} \\
&= 1000 + (50 - 40.672622)a_{\overline{30}|j} \\
&= 1000 + 9.327378 \cdot 17.15168 \\
&= \$1,159.98.
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.23. A used car sells for $9,550. Brent wishes to pay for it in 18 monthly instalments, the first due in three months from the day of purchase. If $12\%$ compounded monthly is charged, determine the size of the monthly payment.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The discounted value of the deferred annuity is

$$
9550 = C \left( \frac{1 - 1.01^{-18}}{0.01} \right) 1.01^{-2} = C \cdot 11.033308.
$$

Hence, the monthly payment is $ C = \frac{9550}{11.033308} \cong \$865.56 $.

standardized_question: Example 1.29. A $1,000 bond that pays interest at $c^{(2)} = 8\%$ is redeemable at par at the end of 5 years. Determine the purchase price to yield an investor $10\%$ compounded semi-annually.
standardized_answer:
Solution. We know that

the redemption value is $W = F = \$1,000$,

the coupon rate is $c = 0.08 / 2 = 0.04$ and the coupon is hence $C = Fc = \$40$,

the number of coupon payments is $n = 5 \cdot 2 = 10$,

the yield rate is $j = 0.1 / 2 = 0.05$.

The purchase price $P$ to yield $i^{(2)} = 10\%$ is the sum of the discounted values of coupons and of the redemption value:

$$
P = 40 \frac{1 - (1 + 0.05)^{-10}}{0.05} + F(1 + 0.05)^{-10} = 308.87 + 613.91 = 892.78.
$$

Since the buyer is buying the bond for less than the redemption value, that is, $P < F$, we say that the bond is purchased at a discount. □

standardized_question: Example 1.32. Investor $\mathbf{A}$ buys a \$2,500 10-year bond paying interest at $c^{(2)} = 6\%$, redeemable at 105, to yield $i^{(2)} = 7\%$. She sells the coupons to investor $\mathbf{B}$, who wishes to yield $i^{(2)} = 6.25\%$, and she sells the strip bond to investor $\mathbf{C}$, who wishes to yield $i^{(4)} = 6.5\%$. What profit does investor A make?
standardized_answer:
Solution. The face value is $F = \$2,500$. The redemption value is $W = 2500 \cdot 1.05 = \$2,625$. Investor $\mathbf{A}$ (with the yield rate $j = 7\% / 2 = 3.5\%$) pays

$$
P_{\mathbf{A}} = 2625 + (2500 \cdot 0.03 - 2625 \cdot 0.035) \cdot a_{20|0.035} = \$2,385.17.
$$

Investor $\mathbf{B}$ (with the yield rate $j = 6.25\% / 2 = 3.125\%$) pays for the coupons

$$
P_{\mathrm{B}} = 2500 \cdot 0.03 \cdot a_{20|0.03125} = \$1,103.02.
$$

Investor $\mathbf{C}$ pays for the strip bond

$$
P_{\mathbf{C}} = 2625 \cdot \left(1 + \frac{0.065}{4}\right)^{-40} = \$1,377.55.
$$

The profit of investor $\mathbf{A}$ is

$$
P_{\mathbf{B}} + P_{\mathbf{C}} - P_{\mathbf{A}} = \$1,103.02 + \$1,377.55 - \$2,385.17 = \$95.40.
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.33. A $5,000 callable bond matures on September 1, 2023, at par. It is callable on September 1, 2018 at $5,250. Interest on the bond is $c^{(2)} = 6\%$. Calculate the price on September 1, 2013, to yield an investor $i^{(2)} = 5\%$.
standardized_answer:
Solution.

Scenario 1: The bond is called prior to maturity. The present value is

$$
P_1 = 5250 + (5000 \cdot 0.03 - 5250 \cdot 0.025) \cdot a_{10\,0.025} = \$5,414.10.
$$

Scenario 2: The bond is not called prior to maturity. The present value is

$$
P_2 = 5000 + 5000 \cdot (0.03 - 0.025) \cdot a_{20\,0.025} = \$5,389.73.
$$

To guarantee that the buyer will yield $i^{(2)} = 5\%$, the purchase price must be the smallest of the two prices:

$$
P = \operatorname*{min}\{P_1, P_2\} = \operatorname*{min}\{5414.10, 5389.73\} = \$5,389.73.
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.36. Compute the yield rate as in the previous example by the method of interpolation.
standardized_answer:
Solution. By the method of averages we determined that the yield rate is approximately $j = 4.16\%$. Now we compute the purchase prices to yield $j = 4\%$ and $j = 4.75\%$ compounded semi-annually. To yield $j = 4\%$ the purchase price is

$$
P = 500 + (23.75 - 20) a_{24|0.04} = \S 557.18.
$$

If the bond interest rate is $c = 9.5\%/2 = 4.75\%$, and the yield rate $j = 4.75\%$, the purchase price is equal to the redemption value: $P = 500$. Assuming that the purchase price $P$ is a linear function of the yield rate $j$, we obtain

$$
\frac{j - 4.75}{4 - 4.75} = \frac{547.50 - 500}{557.18 - 500}
$$

with solution $\begin{aligned} j &= \frac{547.50 - 500}{557.18 - 500} (4 - 4.75) + 4.75 \\ &= 4.75 - 0.75 \cdot \frac{47.5}{57.18} \\ &= 4.127\% \end{aligned}$. So the yield rate is $i^{(2)} = 8.254\%$.

The bond price for a yield $j = 4.127\%$ is $P = 500 + (23.75 - 20.635) a_{24|4.127\%} = \S 547.24$.

standardized_question: Example 1.37. An investor purchases a \$1,000 bond, paying interest at $c^{(2)} = 8\%$ and redeemable at par in 10 years. The bond will yield $i = 7\%$ if held to maturity. After holding the bond for 3 years, the bond is sold to yield the new holder $i^{(2)} = 6\%$. Calculate the investor’s yield rate $i^{(2)}$ over the 3-year investment period.
standardized_answer:
Solution. Using $F c = 1000 \cdot 0.08 / 2 = 40$, $W = 1000$, $n = 10 \cdot 2 = 20$, and $j = 0.035$, we find the purchase price:

$$
\mathrm{Purchase~Price} = 40 a_{\overline{20}|0.035} + 1000 (1.035)^{-20} = \$1,071.06.
$$

After 3 years the selling price can be calculated using $F c = 40$, $W = 1000$, $n = 7 \cdot 2 = 14$, and $j = 0.03$:

$$
\mathrm{Selling~Price} = 40 a_{\overline{14}|0.03} + 1000 (1.03)^{-14} = \$1,112.96.
$$

Now consider the 3-year investment. The investor pays \$1,071.06 for the bond, receives

a \$40 coupon payment every 6 months for 3 years, and then obtains \$1,112.96 when the bond is sold. The equation of value at rate $j$ per half-year is

$$
1071.06 = 40 a_{\overline{6}|j} + 1112.96 (1 + j)^{-6}.
$$

Using the method of averages, an approximate value of the yield rate $j$ is

$$
j \cong \frac{6 \cdot 40 + 1112.96 - 1071.06}{(1112.96 + 1071.06)/2} = 0.043~\text{or}~i^{(2)} = 8.6\%.
$$

By linear interpolation we obtain a more accurate answer. The bond prices for the two yields of 8% and 9% are

$$
\begin{aligned}
P(i^{(2)} = 8\%) &= 40 a_{\overline{6}|0.04} + 1112.96 (1.04)^{-6} = \$1,089.27, \\
P(i^{(2)} = 9\%) &= 40 a_{\overline{6}|0.045} + 1112.96 (1.045)^{-6} = \$1,060.95.
\end{aligned}
$$

Hence for the yield rate $i^{(2)}$ we use interpolation,

$$
\frac{i^{(2)} - 8}{9 - 8} = \frac{1071.06 - 1089.27}{1060.95 - 1089.27} = \frac{18.21}{28.32} = 0.643
$$

giving the yield rate $i^{(2)} = 8.643\%$.

standardized_question:
Example 1.39. Suppose that the continuously compounded yield curve on a zero-coupon bond with $t$ years to maturity is

$$
y(t) = 0.05 - 0.03 \left(1 - \mathrm{e}^{-t}\right)/t, \quad t \geqslant 0.
$$

How much would you pay for a 5-year bond that pays an annual coupon of 3% on a face value of $\$100$?
standardized_answer:
Solution. The cash flows that I receive from the coupon bond (assuming zero credit risk) are no different from the cash flows that I would receive from a portfolio of (i) one zero-coupon bond with face value $\$3$ maturing in one year, (ii) one zero-coupon bond with face value $\$3$ maturing in two years, ..., (v) one zero-coupon bond with face value $\$103$ maturing in five years. Therefore I should pay the same amount for the coupon bond as I would for the portfolio. The cost of the portfolio is

$$
\begin{aligned}
C &= 3 \mathrm{e}^{-y(1) \cdot 1} + 3 \mathrm{e}^{-y(2) \cdot 2} + 3 \mathrm{e}^{-y(3) \cdot 3} + 3 \mathrm{e}^{-y(4) \cdot 4} + 103 \mathrm{e}^{-y(5) \cdot 5} \\
&\cong 3 \mathrm{e}^{-0.031} + 3 \mathrm{e}^{-2 \cdot 0.037} + 3 \mathrm{e}^{-3 \cdot 0.04} + 3 \mathrm{e}^{-4 \cdot 0.043} + 103 \mathrm{e}^{-5 \cdot 0.044} \\
&\cong \$93.52.
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore we should be willing to pay $\$93.52$ for the bond. Using the method of averages we get an approximate yield of

$$
\frac{(3 \cdot 5 + 100 - 93.53)/5}{(93.52 + 100)/2} \cong 0.04439.
$$

standardized_question: Example 3.4. Find an optimal allocation of the initial wealth $V_0 = 1000$ between two risky assets from Example 3.3 when attempting to maximize the expected value, $\mathrm{E}[u(V_T)]$, of an exponential utility function $u(x) = 1 - \mathrm{e}^{-0.01x}$ of the wealth $V_T$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. Let the weights of a portfolio $V$ in the two assets be $w_1 = x$ and $w_2 = 1 - x$, respectively. The return on such a portfolio is $r_V(x) = x r_1 + (1 - x) r_2$. At the end of the period, the portfolio value is $V_T = V_0 (1 + r_V)$. Now we can find the optimal allocation by solving the following maximization problem:

$$
\mathrm{E}[u(V_T)] = \mathrm{E}\left[1 - \mathrm{e}^{-0.01 V_T}\right] = \mathrm{E}\left[1 - \mathrm{e}^{-0.01 V_0 (1 + r_V)}\right] = 1 - \mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{e}^{-10 (1 + x r_1 + (1 - x) r_2)}\right] \to 0.07,
$$

It is equivalent to minimizing $\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{e}^{-10 (1 + x r_1 + (1 - x) r_2)}\right]$ w.r.t. $x$. Evaluate the mathematical expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{E}\left[\mathrm{e}^{-10 (1 + x r_1 + (1 - x) r_2)}\right] &= \sum_{i=1}^{3} p_i \mathrm{e}^{-10 (1 + x r_1(\omega^i) + (1 - x) r_2(\omega^i))} \\
&= 0.1 \mathrm{e}^{-13 + 5x} + 0.6 \mathrm{e}^{-11 + 0.5x} + 0.3 \mathrm{e}^{-8 - 3x}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Differentiate the expected value w.r.t. $x$ and equate the obtained derivative to zero:

$$
0.5 \mathrm{e}^{-13 + 5x} + 0.3 \mathrm{e}^{-11 + 0.5x} - 0.9 \mathrm{e}^{-8 - 3x} = 0.
$$

The resulting equation can be solved numerically to yield the optimal value $x^* \cong 0.67431$, where the expected utility function attains its maximum value. Therefore, the optimal allocation weights are $w_1 \cong 67.431\%$ and $w_2 \cong 32.569\%$. □

standardized_question: Example 4.4. Find the expected value of the gain for a holder of a European put option with strike price $K = \$100$ and exercise date $T = 0.5$ years, if the risk-free continuously compounded rate is $r = 10\%$, the current price of the underlying security is $S(0) = \$95$, the option is bought for $\$17$, and the price $S(0.5)$ may take one of four values: $\$80$, $\$90$, $\$100$, $\$110$, with equal probability.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The expected value of the gain (or loss) to the option holder is the difference between the expected payoff and the appreciated value of the option price paid. The option is in the money only when $S(0.5) = \$80$ or $S(0.5) = \$90$. The respective payoffs are $(100 - 80)^+ = \$20$ and $(100 - 90)^+ = \$10$. The expected gain is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{E}[\mathrm{Gain}] &= -P^E e^{rT} + \mathrm{E}[\mathrm{Payoff}] \\
&= -17 e^{0.1 \cdot 0.5} + 20 \cdot 0.25 + 10 \cdot 0.25 \\
&\cong -17.87 + 5 + 2.50 = -9.37.
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question: Example 1.35. A $500 bond, paying interest at $c^{(2)} = 9.5\%$, redeemable at par on August 15, 2018, is quoted at 109.50 on August 15, 2006. Compute an approximate value of the yield rate compounded semi-annually.
standardized_answer:
Solution. We have $F = W = 500$. The purchase price is $P = 500 \cdot 1.095 = 547.50$ since the bond is sold on a bond interest date. If the buyer holds the bond until maturity, she will receive 24 coupon payments of $\$500 \cdot 0.095 / 2 = 23.75$ each plus the redemption payment of $\$500$. In total the buyer will receive $24 \cdot 23.75 + 500 = 1070$. The net gain $\$1,070 - 547.50 = 522.50$ is realized over 24 interest periods, so that the average interest per period is $\$522.50 / 24 = 21.77$. The average amount invested is $(547.50 + 500) / 2 = \$523.75$. The approximate value of the yield rate is

$$
j = \frac{21.77}{523.75} = 0.0416 = 4.16\% \quad \text{or} \quad i^{(2)} = 8.32\%.
$$

standardized_question: Example 4.5 (Replication and pricing in one period). Consider a single-period binomial model with the following parameters: $S_0 = \mathbb{S}100$, $B_0 = \mathfrak{H}1$, $d = 0.9$, $u = 1.15$, $r = 0.05$. Replicate a call option with strike price $K = \mathbb{S}95$ and expiry time $T = 1$. Find the option price.
standardized_answer:
Solution. Application of (4.9) gives positions $x$ and $y$ of the replicating portfolio for the European call option:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &= \frac{(100 \cdot 1.15 - 95)^+ - (100 \cdot 0.9 - 95)^+}{100 \cdot (1.15 - 0.9)} = \frac{20 - 0}{100 \cdot 0.25} = \frac{4}{5}, \\
y &= \frac{0 \cdot 1.15 - 20 \cdot 0.9}{1 \cdot 1.05 \cdot (1.15 - 0.9)} = \frac{-18}{1.05 \cdot 0.25} \cong -68.5714.
\end{aligned}
$$

So to replicate the European call, we need $\frac{4}{5}$ shares of stock and a loan in the amount of $\$68.57$. The current price of the call option is equal to the portfolio value:

$$
C_0^E = x S_0 + y B_0 \cong \frac{4}{5} \cdot 100 - 68.5714 \cdot 1 \cong \mathbb{S}11.43.
$$

On the other hand, $\tilde{p} = (1.05 - 0.9)/(1.15 - 0.9) = 0.6$, $1 - \tilde{p} = 0.4$ so the risk-neutral pricing formula in (4.10) gives

$$
C_0^E = \frac{1}{1.05} \cdot (20 \cdot 0.6 + 0 \cdot 0.4) = \frac{20 \cdot 0.6}{1.05} \cong \mathbb{S}11.43.
$$

standardized_question: Example 4.9 (Delta-neutral portfolio). An investor writes and sells 1000 one-month call options with strike price $K = \$50$ on stock with an initial price $S_0 = \$50$. Assuming a log-normal price model with $r = 5\%$ and $\sigma = 20\%$, construct a delta-neutral portfolio with initial wealth zero.
standardized_answer:
Solution. Application of (4.25) with $S_0 = \$50$, $K = \$50$, $T = \frac{1}{12}$, $r = 0.05$, and $\sigma = 0.2$ gives the price of one call option, $C^E$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
d_+ &= \frac{\ln\left(\frac{50}{50}\right) + (0.05 + 0.2^2/2) \cdot \frac{1}{12}}{0.2 \sqrt{1/12}} \cong 0.1010363, \\
d_- &= d_+ - 0.2 \sqrt{1/12} \cong 0.0433013, \\
\mathcal{N}(d_+) &\cong 0.54024, \\
\mathcal{N}(d_-) &\cong 0.51727, \\
C^E &= 50 \mathcal{N}(d_-) - e^{-0.05/12} \cdot 50 \mathcal{N}(d_+) \cong \$1.25603.
\end{aligned}
$$

The price of 1000 call options is $1000 C^E \cong 1000 \cdot 1.25603 = \$1256.03$. The delta of one European call is $\Delta = \mathcal{N}(d_+) \cong 0.54024$. Therefore, to construct the hedge, the investor buys $1000 \Delta = 540.24$ stock shares for $50 \cdot 540.24 = \$27,012$ dollars. To cover expenses, the investor borrows $\$27,012 - \$1,256.03 = \$25,755.97$. So the hedging portfolio consists of $x = 540.24$ stock shares, $y = -25,755.97$ dollars in the form of a risk-free loan, and $z = -1000$ short call options. The time-0 value of the portfolio is zero. □

standardized_question: Example 5.8. standardized_question:
Example 5.9. Consider a 3-by-3 model with

$$
\mathbf{D} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 6 & 15 \\ 12 & 8 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad \mathbf{S}_0 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \\ 10 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Suppose that the real-world probabilities are $p_1 = p_3 = \frac{1}{4}$ and $p_2 = \frac{1}{2}$. Find the optimal portfolio $\varphi$ that maximizes $\operatorname{E}[\ln(\Pi_T(\varphi))]$ and has initial value $W_0 = 1$. Find the gain/loss realized.
standardized_answer:
Solution. By solving $\mathbf{D} \Psi = \mathbf{S}_0$, we obtain the state-price vector $\Psi = \left[ \frac{8}{13}, \frac{2}{13}, \frac{3}{13} \right]^\top$. It is strictly positive and unique, hence the model is arbitrage-free and complete. The utility function $u(x) = \ln x$ satisfies the criteria stated above since the derivative $u'(x) = \frac{1}{x}$ varies from $\infty$ to $0$ as $x \nearrow \infty$ and $x \searrow 0$. Substituting the inverse $v(y) = \frac{1}{y}$ into (5.28) gives the optimal payoff $\mathbf{X}^*$ in terms of $\lambda^*$:

$$
x_j = \frac{p_j}{\lambda^* \Psi_j}, \quad j = 1, 2, 3 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \mathbf{X}^* = \frac{1}{\lambda^*} \left[ \frac{13}{32}, \frac{13}{4}, \frac{13}{12} \right].
$$

Solving (5.27) with $W_0 = 1$ for $\lambda$ gives

$$
1 = \sum_{j=1}^3 \frac{p_j}{\lambda \Psi_j} \Psi_j = \frac{1}{\lambda} \sum_{j=1}^3 p_j = \frac{1}{\lambda} \implies \lambda^* = 1.
$$

Therefore, the optimal payoff vector is $\mathbf{X}^* = \left[ \frac{13}{32}, \frac{13}{4}, \frac{13}{12} \right]$. Solving the matrix-vector equation gives the optimal allocation portfolio:

$$
\boldsymbol{\varphi}^* = \left[ \frac{853}{48}, -\frac{53}{96}, -\frac{269}{192} \right].
$$

The gain of the investment is $\mathbf{X}^* - W_0 = \left[ -\frac{19}{32}, \frac{9}{4}, \frac{1}{12} \right]$. So the return on the investment is only positive in states $\omega^2$ and $\omega^3$.

standardized_question: Example 5.11. Consider the trinomial model from Example 5.10. Find the no-arbitrage initial price of a long forward contract $F$ with the forward price $K = \mathbb{S}100$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The payoff of a long forward contract is attainable as it is replicated by a portfolio consisting of one long position in the stock and a loan in the amount of $K$ :

$$
F_T := S_T - K = S_T - K B_T.
$$

The initial price $F_0$ of the forward contract is unique and equal to

$$
F_0 = S_0 - K B_0 = S_0 - \frac{K}{1 + r} = 100 - \frac{100}{1.2} = \frac{50}{3} \cong \mathfrak{H}16.67.
$$

On the other hand, we know that the risk-neutral pricing formula (5.16) must give us the same initial value of the contract regardless of the choice of the risk-neutral probability measure $\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(c)$ with $c \in (0, \frac{5}{9})$. Using the probabilities in (5.35) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
&= \frac{1}{1 + r} \mathrm{E}^{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(c)}[F_T] = \frac{1}{1 + r} \sum_{j=1}^{3} \left( S_T(\omega^j) - K \right) \widetilde{p}_j(c) \\
&= \frac{1}{1.2} \left( (80 - 100) \cdot \frac{1 - v}{3} + (110 - 100) \cdot \frac{2v}{3} + (140 - 100) \cdot \frac{2 - \upsilon}{3} \right) \\
&= \frac{-20(1 - v) + 20v + 40(2 - v)}{3.6} = \frac{-20 + 20v + 20v + 80 - 40v}{3.6} \\
&= \frac{60}{3.6} = \frac{50}{3} \cong \mathfrak{H}6.67,
\end{aligned}
$$

where $v = \frac{9c}{5} \in (0, 1)$. Alternatively, using the pricing formula (5.13) and solution (5.34) gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_0 &= \sum_{j=1}^{3} F_T(\omega^j) \Psi_j(c) = (-20) \cdot \left( \frac{5}{18} - \frac{c}{2} \right) + 10 \cdot c + 40 \cdot \left( \frac{5}{9} - \frac{c}{2} \right) \\
&= (10 + 10 - 20)c + \frac{200 - 50}{9} = \frac{50}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question: Example 4.6 (Pricing in two periods). Consider the two-period binomial model from Example 4.5. Find the no-arbitrage prices $C_0^E$ and $C_1^E$ of the call price with the strike price $K = \mathbb{S}95$ and expiry time $T = 2$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. First, compute the risk-neutral probabilities:

$$
\tilde{p} = \frac{1.05 - 0.9}{1.15 - 0.9} = 0.6, \quad 1 - \tilde{p} = 0.4.
$$

Second, we calculate the prices $C_1^E(S_1)$ when $S_1 = S_0 u = \mathbb{S}115$ and $S_1 = S_0 d = \mathbb{S}90$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_1^E(90) &= \frac{1}{1 + r} \left( \Lambda(90u) \tilde{p} + \Lambda(90d) (1 - \tilde{p}) \right) \\
&= \frac{1}{1.05} \cdot \left( (90 \cdot 1.15 - 95)^+ \cdot 0.6 + (90 \cdot 0.9 - 95)^+ \cdot 0.4 \right) \\
&= \frac{8.5 \cdot 0.6 + 0 \cdot 0.4}{1.05} \cong 4.85714, \\
C_1^E(115) &= \frac{1}{1.05} \cdot \left( (115 \cdot 1.15 - 95)^+ \cdot 0.6 + (115 \cdot 0.9 - 95)^+ \cdot 0.4 \right) \\
&= \frac{37.25 \cdot 0.6 + 8.5 \cdot 0.4}{1.05} \cong 24.52381.
\end{aligned}
$$

Third, calculate $C_0^E(100)$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_0^E(100) &= \frac{1}{1 + r} \left( C_1^E(100u) \tilde{p} + C_1^E(100d) (1 - \tilde{p}) \right) \\
&\cong \frac{1}{1.05} \cdot (24.52381 \cdot 0.6 + 4.85714 \cdot 0.4) \\
&= \frac{15.86394}{1.05} \cong 15.86394.
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question: Example 5.13. Consider the trinomial (incomplete) model from Example 5.10. Find the bid-ask spread for the initial price of the call option with strike $K = 120$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The first approach is to solve the super- and sub-replication problems given by (5.38) and (5.40), respectively,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\Pi_0[\varphi^d] \to \max_{\varphi^d \in \mathbb{R}^2} & \iff \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\frac{5}{6} \varphi_1^d + 100 \varphi_2^d \to \max_{[\varphi^d, \varphi^d] \in \mathbb{R}^2} \\
\varphi_1^d + 80 \varphi_2^d \in 0,
\end{array} \right. \\
\Pi_T[\varphi^d] \leqslant X & \iff \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\varphi_1^d + 10 \varphi_2^d \leqslant 10, \\
\varphi_1^d + 110 \varphi_2^d \leqslant 40
\end{array} \right. \\
\varphi_1^d + 140 \varphi_2^d \leqslant 40
\end{array} \right. \\
\left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\Pi_0[\varphi^u] \to \min_{\varphi^u \in \mathbb{R}^2} \\
\Pi_T[\varphi^u] \geqslant X
\end{array} \right. & \iff \left\{ \begin{array}{ll}
\frac{5}{6} \varphi_1^u + 100 \varphi_2^u \to \min_{[\varphi^u, \varphi_2^u] \in \mathbb{R}^2} \\
\varphi_1^u + 80 \varphi_2^u \geqslant 0, \\
\varphi_1^u + 110 \varphi_2^u \geqslant 10 \\
\varphi_1^u + 140 \varphi_2^u \geqslant 40
\end{array} \right.
\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions to the linear programming problems (5.45) and (5.46) are, respectively,

$$
\varphi^d = [-100, 1] \quad \text{and} \quad \varphi^u = \left[-53\frac{1}{3}, \frac{2}{3}\right].
$$

The bid price $\pi_0^d$ and ask price $\pi_0^u$ of the call option are then given by

$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi_0^d &= \Pi_0[\varphi^d] = -100 \cdot \frac{5}{6} + 1 \cdot 100 = \frac{50}{3} \cong \mathfrak{F}16.67, \\
\pi_0^u &= \Pi_0[\varphi^u] = -53\frac{1}{3} \cdot \frac{5}{6} + \frac{2}{3} \cdot 100 = \frac{200}{9} \cong \mathfrak{F}22.22.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the bid-ask spread is $(16.67, 22.22)$.

The other approach is to find the bid-ask spread by computing the extreme values of the risk-neutral expectation of the discounted payoff. Since the mathematical expectation of a random variable from $\mathcal{L}(\Omega)$ is a linear function of the state probabilities, the maximum and minimum in (5.43) and (5.44) are attained at the endpoints of the domain $\{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}\}$. Therefore, we just need to calculate the expected value

$$
\pi_0(c) = \frac{1}{1 + r} \mathrm{E}^{\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(c)}[(S_T - K)^+] = \frac{1}{1 + r} \sum_{j=1}^3 \widetilde{p}_j(c) (S_T(\omega^j) - K)^+
$$

using risk-neutral probabilities given by (5.35) with extreme values $c = 0$ and $c = \frac{5}{9}$. The bid price is the smaller of the two prices calculated, and the ask price is the larger one. The above expectation is calculated explicitly in the measure $\widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(v)$:

$$
\pi_0\left(\frac{5v}{9}\right) = \frac{5}{6} \cdot \left(0 \cdot \frac{1 - v}{3} + 10 \cdot \frac{2v}{3} + 40 \cdot \frac{2 - v}{3}\right) = \frac{50(4 - v)}{9}, \quad 0 \leqslant v \leqslant 1.
$$

The extreme values are $\min\left\{\frac{200}{9}, \frac{50}{3}\right\} = \frac{50}{3}$ and the ask price is $\pi_0(v = 0) = \frac{200}{9}$, $\max\left\{\frac{200}{9}, \frac{50}{3}\right\} = \frac{200}{9}$ and $\pi_0(v = 1) = \frac{50}{3} = \frac{150}{9}$. As required, both prices agree with the values obtained using the first approach.

In the conclusion of this section, let us consider an example of a single-period model with four states of the world and two tradable assets.

standardized_question: Example 6.12. Consider a four-period binomial model with $p = \frac{1}{2}$. Find $\mathrm{E}[\mathsf{U}_4 \mid B]$ for $B = \left\{ \text{at least two } \mathsf{U}\text{s} \right\}$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The event $B \subset \Omega_4$ can be characterized by listing all elements $\omega = \omega_1 \omega_2 \omega_3 \omega_4$ of its complement:

$$
B^\complement = \{ \omega \mid \mathsf{U}_4(\omega) \leqslant 1 \} = \{ \mathsf{DDD D}, \mathsf{DDDU}, \mathsf{DDUD}, \mathsf{D UDD}, \mathsf{UDDD} \}.
$$

Note that all outcomes in $\Omega_4$ are all equally likely since $p = 1 - p = \frac{1}{2}$; the probability of each particular scenario is $\left( \frac{1}{2} \right)^4 = \frac{1}{16}$. First, calculate $\mathbb{P}(B)$:

$$
\mathbb{P}(B) = 1 - \mathbb{P}(B^\complement) = 1 - 5 \cdot \frac{1}{16} = \frac{11}{16}.
$$

Second, apply (6.19) to calculate $\mathrm{E}[\mathsf{U}_4 \mid B]$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{E}[\mathsf{U}_4 \mathbb{I}_B] &= \sum_{\omega \in B} \mathsf{U}_4(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\omega) = \sum_{\omega : \mathsf{U}_4(\omega) \geqslant 2} \mathsf{U}_4(\omega) \mathbb{P}(\omega) = \sum_{k=2}^{4} k \cdot \mathbb{P}(\mathsf{U}_4 = k) \\
&= \frac{1}{16} \cdot \left( 2 \cdot \binom{4}{2} + 3 \cdot \binom{4}{3} + 4 \cdot \binom{4}{4} \right) = \frac{1}{16} \cdot (2 \cdot 6 + 3 \cdot 4 + 4 \cdot 1) = \frac{28}{16} = \frac{7}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, $\mathrm{E}[\mathsf{U}_4 \mid B] = \mathrm{E}[\mathsf{U}_4 \mathbb{I}_B] / \mathbb{P}(B) = \frac{7/4}{11/16} = \frac{28}{11}$.

standardized_question: Example 7.1. Consider a three-period recombining binomial tree model with $S_0 = 8$, $B_0 = 1$, $u = \frac{3}{2}$, $d = \frac{1}{2}$, and $r = \frac{1}{4}$. Find the terminal value of a self-financing strategy with the initial value $\Pi_0 = 10$ and stock positions $\Delta_t$ given as the number of upward moves in the first $t$ market movements for each $t = 0, 1, 2$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The recombining binomial tree for the stock price process is given in Figure 7.1. Now construct the self-financing strategy and calculate its value step by step going forward in time. Note that the positions $\Delta_0 = 0$, $\Delta_1 = \# \mathsf{U}(\omega_1)$, $\Delta_2 = \# \mathsf{U}(\omega_1\omega_2)$ are $\mathcal{F}_0$-, $\mathcal{F}_1$-, and $\mathcal{F}_2$-measurable, respectively. The self-financing investment strategy is therefore adapted to the natural filtration. Construct the strategy for each $t = 0, 1, 2$ as follows.

![](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2025-09-28/70c52890-2387-4342-9bd7-2569363f49bd/778ebeb64518268cf15ff86014858c14d8a31ceb4f9fd6f031c7309bad5de401.jpg)  
FIGURE 7.1: A three-period recombining binomial tree.

$t = 0$: Since $\Delta_0 = 0$, at time 0 all the capital is invested in the bank account with $\beta_0 = \Pi_0 = 10$.

$t = 1$: There are no shares of stock in our investment portfolio so far. Therefore, its value is independent of $\omega_1$ and by the above wealth equation:

$$
\Pi_1 = \beta_0 B_1 = \Pi_0 \cdot (1 + r) = 12.5.
$$

If $\omega_1 = \mathsf{D}$, then $\Delta_1(\mathsf{D}) = 0$ and $\beta_1(\mathsf{D}) = \beta_0 = 10$. If $\omega_1 = \mathsf{U}$, then $\Delta_1(\mathsf{U}) = 1$ and

$$
\beta_1(\mathsf{U}) = \frac{\Pi_1(\mathsf{U}) - S_1(\mathsf{U}) \Delta_1(\mathsf{U})}{B_1} = \frac{12.5 - 12 \cdot 1}{1.25} = 0.4.
$$

$t = 2$: The self-financed portfolio has value $\Pi_2(\omega_1\omega_2) = \beta_1(\omega_1) B_2 + \Delta_1(\omega_1) S_2(\omega_1\omega_2)$ for each of four scenarios: $\omega_1\omega_2 \in \{\mathsf{DD}, \mathsf{DU}, \mathsf{UD}, \mathsf{UU}\}$. Let us calculate the respective liquidation values of $\Delta_2$ and $\beta_2$ in each case.

• If $\omega_1\omega_2 = \mathsf{DD}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_2(\mathsf{DD}) &= \beta_1(\mathsf{D}) B_2 + \Delta_1(\mathsf{D}) S_2(\mathsf{DD}) = 10 \cdot 1.25^2 + 0 \cdot 2 = 15.625, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{DD}) &= \# \mathsf{U}(\mathsf{DD}) = 0, \\
\beta_2(\mathsf{DD}) &= \frac{\Pi_2(\mathsf{DD}) - S_2(\mathsf{DD}) \Delta_2(\mathsf{DD})}{B_2} = \frac{15.625 - 2 \cdot 0}{1.25^2} = 10.
\end{aligned}
$$

• If $\omega_1\omega_2 = \mathsf{DU}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_2(\mathsf{DU}) &= \beta_1(\mathsf{D}) B_2 + \Delta_1(\mathsf{D}) S_2(\mathsf{DU}) = 10 \cdot 1.25^2 + 0 \cdot 6 = 15.625, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{DU}) &= \# \mathsf{U}(\mathsf{DU}) = 1, \\
\beta_2(\mathsf{DU}) &= \frac{\Pi_2(\mathsf{DU}) - S_2(\mathsf{DU}) \Delta_2(\mathsf{DU})}{B_2} = \frac{15.625 - 6 \cdot 1}{1.25^2} = 6.16.
\end{aligned}
$$

• If $\omega_1\omega_2 = \mathsf{UD}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_2(\mathsf{UD}) &= \beta_1(\mathsf{U}) B_2 + \Delta_1(\mathsf{U}) S_2(\mathsf{UD}) = 0.4 \cdot 1.25^2 + 1 \cdot 6 = 6.625, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{UD}) &= \# \mathsf{U}(\mathsf{UD}) = 1, \\
\beta_2(\mathsf{UD}) &= \frac{\Pi_2(\mathsf{UD}) - S_2(\mathsf{UD}) \Delta_2(\mathsf{UD})}{B_2} = \frac{6.625 - 6 \cdot 1}{1.25^2} = 0.4.
\end{aligned}
$$

• If $\omega_1\omega_2 = \mathsf{UU}$, then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi_2(\mathsf{UU}) &= \beta_1(\mathsf{U}) B_2 + \Delta_1(\mathsf{U}) S_2(\mathsf{UU}) = 0.4 \cdot 1.25^2 + 1 \cdot 18 = 18.625, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{UU}) &= \# \mathsf{U}(\mathsf{UU}) = 2, \\
\beta_2(\mathsf{UU}) &= \frac{\Pi_2(\mathsf{UU}) - S_2(\mathsf{UU}) \Delta_2(\mathsf{UU})}{B_2} = \frac{18.625 - 18 \cdot 2}{1.25^2} = -11.12.
\end{aligned}
$$

The terminal value $\Pi_3$ of the strategy is calculated by

$$
\Pi_3(\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3) = \beta_2(\omega_1\omega_2) B_3 + \Delta_2(\omega_1\omega_2) S_3(\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3), \quad \omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3 \in \{\mathsf{D}, \mathsf{U}\}.
$$

The full details of this three-period strategy, for every scenario, are summarized in Figure 7.2. □

standardized_question:
Example 7.4. Consider a binomial tree model from Example 7.1. Determine the prices and replicating strategy for a lookback call option with payoff

$$
X = S_3 - \min_{0 \leqslant t \leqslant 3} S_t.
$$
standardized_answer:
Solution. First, we shall construct a tree of possible scenarios. To calculate the payoff function at maturity $T = 3$ we need to know the minimum price

$$
m_3(\omega) = \min_{0 \leqslant t \leqslant 3} S_t(\omega)
$$

for all market scenarios $\omega \in \Omega_3$. The sampled minimum $m_t = \min_{0 \leqslant n \leqslant t} S_n$, $t = 0, 1, 2, 3$, can be calculated simultaneously with stock prices using the formula $m_t = \min\{m_{t-1}, S_t\}$, $t = 1, 2, 3$, where $m_0 = S_0$. Since the value of $m_t$ depends on the historical path of the stock price process (i.e., a market scenario $\omega$), the result can be represented using a nonrecombining scenario tree, as given in Figure 7.3. As is clearly seen from Figure 7.3, the tree cannot be reduced to a recombining one since $m_2(\mathrm{DU}) \ne m_2(\mathrm{UD})$, $m_3(\mathrm{UUD}) \ne m_3(\mathrm{UDU}) \ne m_3(\mathrm{DUU})$, etc.

To calculate the derivative prices $V_t$, $t = 0, 1, 2$, we first evaluate the payoff function

$$
V_3(\omega) = S_3(\omega) - m_3(\omega)
$$

for all eight possible scenarios $\omega \in \Omega_3$. After that, using the backward recursion (7.16) with

![](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2025-09-28/70c52890-2387-4342-9bd7-2569363f49bd/b0d602db4a57bd6c847225e6f9fb71994a49178d2bbe83b3e32ae1527a0e64c0.jpg)  
FIGURE 7.3: A binomial tree with stock prices $S$ and sampled minimum values $m$ calculated for each node. There are $|\Omega_3| = 8$ distinct paths from time 0 to 3.

![](https://cdn-mineru.openxlab.org.cn/result/2025-09-28/70c52890-2387-4342-9bd7-2569363f49bd/cef16c6e5fcc5de77861c3073c5d25f4d042ed8cbbc54c0923d12bdc428ed784.jpg)  
FIGURE 7.4: A scenario tree with derivative prices calculated for each node of a three-period nonrecombining tree.

$$
\tilde{p} = \frac{3}{4},\quad r = \frac{1}{4}
$$

we compute derivative prices as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_2(\omega_1\omega_2) &= \frac{1}{1 + r} \left( \tilde{p} V_3(\omega_1\omega_2\mathsf{U}) + (1 - \tilde{p}) V_3(\omega_1\omega_2\mathsf{D}) \right) \\
&= \frac{3 V_3(\omega_1\omega_2\mathsf{U}) + V_3(\omega_1\omega_2\mathsf{D})}{5}, \\
V_1(\omega_1) &= \frac{1}{1 + r} \left( \tilde{p} V_2(\omega_1\mathsf{U}) + (1 - \tilde{p}) V_2(\omega_1\mathsf{D}) \right) \\
&= \frac{3 V_2(\omega_1\mathsf{U}) + V_2(\omega_1\mathsf{D})}{5}, \\
V_0 &= \frac{1}{1 + r} \left( \tilde{p} V_1(\mathsf{U}) + (1 - \tilde{p}) V_1(\mathsf{D}) \right) \\
&= \frac{3 V_1(\mathsf{U}) + V_1(\mathsf{D})}{5},
\end{aligned}
$$

where $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \{\mathsf{D}, \mathsf{U}\}$. The results of our computations are summarized in Figure 7.4.

We can now also obtain the replicating strategy using the delta hedging formula in (7.19) for $\Delta_t$, $t = 0, 1, 2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_0 &= \frac{V_1(\mathbf{U}) - V_1(\mathbf{D})}{S_1(\mathbf{U}) - S_1(\mathbf{D})} = \frac{3.32 - 1.92}{12 - 4} = \frac{1.4}{8} = 0.175, \\
\Delta_1(\mathsf{U}) &= \frac{V_2(\mathsf{UU}) - V_2(\mathsf{UD})}{S_2(\mathsf{UU}) - S_2(\mathsf{UD})}, \\
\Delta_1(\mathsf{D}) &= \frac{V_2(\mathsf{DU}) - V_2(\mathsf{DD})}{S_2(\mathsf{DU}) - S_2(\mathsf{DD})}, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{UU}) &= \frac{V_3(\mathsf{UUU}) - V_3(\mathsf{UUD})}{S_3(\mathsf{UUU}) - S_3(\mathsf{UUD})}, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{UD}) &= \frac{V_3(\mathsf{UDU}) - V_3(\mathsf{UDD})}{S_3(\mathsf{UDU}) - S_3(\mathsf{UDD})}, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{DU}) &= \frac{V_3(\mathsf{DUU}) - V_3(\mathsf{DUD})}{S_3(\mathsf{DUU}) - S_3(\mathsf{DUD})}, \\
\Delta_2(\mathsf{DD}) &= \frac{V_3(\mathsf{DDU}) - V_3(\mathsf{DDD})}{S_3(\mathsf{DDU}) - S_3(\mathsf{DDD})}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The alternative method for computing the derivative prices is to use (7.28). For example, the initial price can be computed by the following discounted expectation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_0 &= (1 + r)^{-3} \widetilde{\mathrm{E}}[V_3] = (1 + r)^{-3} \sum_{\omega \in \Omega_3} \widetilde{\mathbb{P}}(\omega) V_3(\omega) \\
&= \left( \frac{5}{4} \right)^{-3} \sum_{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3 \in \{\mathsf{U}, \mathsf{D}\}} \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^{\#\{ \omega_1\omega_2\omega_3 \mid \omega_i = \mathsf{U} \}} \left( \frac{1}{4} \right)^{\#\{ \omega_1\omega_2\omega_3 \mid \omega_i = \mathsf{D} \}} V_3(\omega_1\omega_2\omega_3) \\
&= \left( \frac{4}{5} \right)^3 \left\{ 19 \cdot \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^3 + (5 + 3) \cdot \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^2 \frac{1}{4} + 1 \cdot \left[ \left( \frac{3}{4} \right)^2 \frac{1}{4} + \left( \frac{1}{4} \right)^2 \frac{3}{4} \right] \right\} \\
&= 4.776.
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question: Example 7.6. Consider the three-period model in Example 7.1 with $u = \frac{3}{2}$, $d = \frac{1}{2}$, $r = \frac{1}{4}$, $T = 3$. Find prices for the floating strike lookback call option with payoff as in Example 7.4.
standardized_answer:
Solution. The nodes $(S, m)$ at each time $t = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are displayed in Figure 7.3. Beginning with time $t = 3$, we have seven distinct pairs of values:

$$
(S_3, m_3) = (S, m) \in \{ (27, 8), (9, 8), (9, 6), (9, 4), (3, 3), (3, 2), (1, 1) \}.
$$

The derivative price at those nodes is simply the payoff value, $V_3(S, m) = \Lambda(S, m) = S - m$

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_3(27, 8) &= 19, \quad V_3(9, 8) = 1, \quad V_3(9, 6) = 3, \quad V_3(9, 4) = 5, \\
V_3(3, 3) &= 0, \quad V_3(3, 2) = 1, \quad V_3(1, 1) = 0.
\end{aligned}
$$

The nodes at time $t = 2$ are $(S_2, m_2) = (S, m) \in \{ (18, 8), (6, 6), (6, 4), (2, 2) \}$. Equation (7.59) with $\tilde{p} = \frac{3}{4}$ now reads

$$
V_t(S, m) = \frac{3}{5} V_{t+1} \left( \frac{3S}{2}, m \wedge \frac{3S}{2} \right) + \frac{1}{5} V_{t+1} \left( \frac{S}{2}, m \wedge \frac{S}{2} \right).
$$

Applying this equation for $t = 2$ to all four nodes and using the above payoff values gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
V_2(18, 8) &= \frac{3}{5} V_3(27, 8) + \frac{1}{5} V_3(9, 8) = 11.60; \\
V_2(6, 6) &= \frac{3}{5} V_3(9, 6) + \frac{1}{5} V_3(3, 3) = 1.80; \\
V_2(6, 4) &= \frac{3}{5} V_3(9, 4) + \frac{1}{5} V_3(3, 3) = 3.00; \\
V_2(2, 2) &= \frac{3}{5} V_3(3, 2) + \frac{1}{5} V_3(1, 1) = 0.60.
\end{aligned}
$$

Applying again the recurrence formula for $t = 1$ to the two nodes $(S_1, m_1) = (S, m) \in \{ (12, 8), (4, 4) \}$:

$$
V_1(12, 8) = \frac{3}{5} V_2(18, 8) + \frac{1}{5} V_2(6, 6) = 7.32; \quad V_1(4, 4) = \frac{3}{5} V_2(6, 4) + \frac{1}{5} V_2(2, 2) = 1.92.
$$

Finally, the price at current time $t = 0$ is calculated for $(S_0, m_0) = (S_0, S_0) = (8, 8)$

$$
V_0(8, 8) = \frac{3}{5} V_1(12, 8) + \frac{1}{5} V_1(4, 4) = 4.776.
$$

Note that this agrees with the price $V_0$ in Example 7.4 which was computed by two other methods. □

standardized_question: Example 7.5. Consider the three-period recombining binomial tree model from Example 7.1 with $S_0 = 8$, $B_0 = 1$, $\textstyle u = \frac{3}{2}$, $\textstyle d = \frac{1}{2}$, and $\textstyle r = \frac{1}{4}$. Determine the option prices and replication strategy for a standard European call with maturity time $T = 3$ and strike price $K = 8$ (i.e., the call option is at the money).
standardized_answer:
Solution. We first calculate the payoff values and then the call option prices $C_t(S_{t,n})$ at $t = 0, 1, 2$ using the backward-in-time recursion (7.34), which takes the following form:

$$
C_t(S_{t,n}) = \frac{1}{1 + r} \left( \tilde{p} C_{t+1}(S_{t,n}u) + (1 - \tilde{p}) C_{t+1}(S_{t,n}d) \right) = \frac{3 C_{t+1}(S_{t,n}u) + C_{t+1}(S_{t,n}d)}{5}
$$

where $S_{t,n} = S_0 u^n d^{t-n} = 8 \cdot 1.5^n \cdot 0.5^{t-n}$ for $n = 0, 1, \ldots, t$

$t = 3$: At maturity $T = 3$, calculate the payoff values $C_3(S_3) = (S_3 - 8)^+$, where $S_3 \in \{1, 3, 9, 27\}$:

$$
C_3(1) = C_3(3) = 0, \quad C_3(9) = 1, \quad C_3(27) = 19.
$$

$t = 2$: Calculate the option prices at time $t = 2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
C_2(2) &= \frac{3 C_3(3) + C_3(1)}{5} = 0, \\
C_2(6) &= \frac{3 C_3(9) + C_3(3)}{5} = 0.6, \\
C_2(18) &= \frac{3 C_3(27) + C_3(9)}{5} = 11.6.
\end{aligned}
$$

$t = 1$: Calculate the option prices at time $t = 1$:

$$
C_1(4) = \frac{3 C_2(6) + C_2(2)}{5} = 0.36, \quad C_1(12) = \frac{3 C_2(18) + C_2(6)}{5} = 7.08.
$$

$t = 0$: The initial option price is

$$
C_0(8) = \frac{3 C_1(12) + C_1(4)}{5} = 4.32.
$$

Now, compute the replication strategy $\{(\beta_t, \Delta_t)\}_{t=0,1,2}$ using the formulae (7.37) and (7.38):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_0(8) &= \frac{C_1(12) - C_1(4)}{12 - 4} = 0.84, & \beta_0(8) &= \frac{C_0(8) - 8 \Delta_0(8)}{1} = -2.4, \\
\Delta_1(4) &= \frac{C_2(6) - C_2(2)}{6 - 2} = 0.15, & \beta_1(4) &= \frac{C_1(4) - 4 \Delta_1(4)}{1.25} = -0.192, \\
\Delta_1(12) &= \frac{C_2(18) - C_2(6)}{18 - 12} = \frac{11}{12} \geq 0.9167, & \beta_1(12) &= \frac{C_1(12) - 12 \Delta_1(12)}{1.25} = -3.136, \\
\Delta_2(2) &= \frac{C_3(3) - C_3(1)}{3 - 1} = 0, & \beta_2(2) &= \frac{C_2(2) - 2 \Delta_2(2)}{1.25^2} = 0, \\
\Delta_2(6) &= \frac{C_3(9) - C_3(3)}{9 - 3} = \frac{1}{6} \cong 0.1667, & \beta_2(6) &= \frac{C_2(6) - 6 \Delta_2(6)}{1.25^2} = -0.256.
\end{aligned}
$$

standardized_question:
Example 11.10. Solve the boundary value problem:

$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} = 0,
$$

for $x \in \mathbb{R}, 0 \leqslant t \leqslant T$, subject to $f(x, T) = \phi(x)$ where $\phi$ is an arbitrary function. Give the explicit solution for $\phi(x) = x^2$.
standardized_answer:
Solution. Observe that this PDE is of the same form as in (11.49) with coefficient functions $\sigma(t, x) \equiv 1, \mu(t, x) \equiv 0$. The corresponding SDE in (11.24) is then

$$
\mathrm{d}X(t) = \mathrm{d}W(t).
$$

This trivial linear SDE has the solution $X(t) = x_0 + W(t)$. As seen below, the end result does not depend on $x_0$ since $X(T) - X(t) = W(T) - W(t)$. Using (11.50) and the fact that $W(T) - W(t)$ and $W(t)$ are independent, the solution takes the equivalent forms

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(t, x) &= \mathrm{E}[\phi(X(T)) \mid X(t) = x] \\
&= \mathrm{E}[\phi(W(T) - W(t) + X(t)) \mid X(t) = x] \\
&= \mathrm{E}[\phi(W(T) - W(t) + x)] \\
&= \mathrm{E}[\phi(W(T)) \mid W(t) = x] \\
&= \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} \phi(y) p(t, T; x, y) \, dy, \quad \text{for } t < T,
\end{aligned}
$$

where 
$$
p(t, T; x, y) := \frac{\mathrm{e}^{-\frac{(y - x)^2}{2(T - t)}}}{\sqrt{2\pi(T - t)}}
$$
is the transition PDF of standard Brownian motion. The last line follows immediately from (10.13). Note that, for $t = T$, the boundary value condition is satisfied where $f(T, x) = \mathrm{E}[\phi(W(T) - W(T) + x)] = \mathrm{E}[\phi(x)] = \phi(x)$.

For $\phi(x) = x^2$, we simply have

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(t, x) &= \mathrm{E}[(W(T) - W(t) + x)^2] \\
&= \mathrm{E}[(W(T) - W(t))^2] + 2x\mathrm{E}[W(T) - W(t)] + x^2 \\
&= (T - t) + x^2,
\end{aligned}
$$

for all $0 \leqslant t \leqslant T$. Note that the terminal condition is satisfied, $f(T, x) = x^2$, and this function satisfies the above PDE since
$$
\frac{\partial f}{\partial t} + \frac{1}{2} \frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x^2} = -1 + \frac{1}{2}(2) = 0.
$$
□
